title: We Have Waited for Him, and He Will Save Us
sections: Symbols can help me remember Jesus Christ

sayings.text: My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering
sayings.speaker: Abraham, to Isaac
sayings.why: Isaac had asked, “where is the lamb for a burnt offering?” (Genesis 22:7). Abraham’s answer pointed ahead to the Lamb of God.

sayings.text: I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but not nigh
sayings.speaker: Balaam, about a coming King
sayings.why: Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel, but Balaam blessed them instead and saw “a Star out of Jacob” far in the future.

sayings.text: Lo, this is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us
sayings.speaker: God’s people, in that day
sayings.why: The verse begins, “And it shall be said in that day.” This week’s title is what God’s people will say when He comes.

sayings.text: Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy
sayings.speaker: An angel, to shepherds
sayings.why: The angel came to shepherds “keeping watch over their flock by night” (Luke 2:8) and told them the Savior was born.

sayings.text: Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east
sayings.speaker: Wise men, in Jerusalem
sayings.why: Wise men from the east came looking for the newborn King. Long before, Balaam had seen “a Star out of Jacob” (Numbers 24:17).

sayings.text: In Bethlehem of Judæa: for thus it is written by the prophet
sayings.speaker: Chief priests and scribes, to Herod
sayings.why: Herod asked where Christ should be born. They answered with the prophecy of Micah (Micah 5:2).

sayings.text: Were it not for our transgression we never should have had seed
sayings.speaker: Eve, after the Fall
sayings.why: Eve was glad when she learned of “the joy of our redemption.” The Fall opened the way for families and for a Redeemer.

sayings.text: Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word
sayings.speaker: Mary, to the angel Gabriel
sayings.why: Gabriel told Mary she would have a son and “call his name JESUS” (Luke 1:31). Mary answered with faith.

sayings.text: I am Messiah, the King of Zion, the Rock of Heaven
sayings.speaker: The Lord, to Enoch
sayings.why: The Lord showed Enoch a vision of the Savior’s coming and used these titles for Himself. Messiah means the Anointed One.

words.clue: For unto you is born this day in the city of David a ____, which is Christ the Lord.
words.mean: The baby born in Bethlehem was the Savior and Lord the prophets had promised.

words.clue: And my soul shall be joyful in the LORD: it shall ____ in his salvation.
words.mean: David’s soul was full of joy because the Lord saves.

words.clue: there shall come a ____ out of Jacob
words.mean: Balaam saw that a King, Jesus Christ, would come from Jacob’s family like a rising star.

words.clue: The everlasting Father, The Prince of ____.
words.mean: Jesus brings peace to our hearts now, and one day He will bring it to the whole earth.

words.clue: God will provide himself a ____ for a burnt offering
words.mean: Abraham’s words pointed to Jesus Christ, the Lamb of God, whom Heavenly Father would give.

words.clue: and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a ____
words.mean: The Son of God was born in a humble place and laid in a feeding box for animals.

words.clue: The people that walked in darkness have seen a great ____
words.mean: Jesus Christ is the great light Isaiah saw coming: the Light of the World.

deep.intro: The lesson lists Isaiah 44:21–24 among passages that gave Israel joy as they waited for the Savior. Read what the Lord did for His people, and who sings about it.
deep.q: In Isaiah 44:23, besides the heavens, what does Isaiah call on to sing?
deep.hunt: In Isaiah 44, besides the heavens, what does Isaiah call on to sing?
deep.right: The mountains, the forest and every tree
wrong: The priests, the Levites and the singers
The kings, the princes and the judges
deep.why: Verse 23: “break forth into singing, ye mountains, O forest, and every tree therein: for the LORD hath redeemed Jacob.” All creation rejoices in the Redeemer.
deep.find: break forth into singing, ye mountains, O forest, and every tree therein

deep.intro: The lesson points to 2 Nephi 11:4 to show why the Old Testament is full of symbols of Christ. Read why Nephi loved Isaiah’s words.
deep.q: In 2 Nephi 11:4, what does Nephi say all things given of God from the beginning of the world are?
deep.hunt: In 2 Nephi 11, what does Nephi say all things given of God from the beginning of the world are?
wrong: Tests to see who would obey
deep.why: Verse 4: all things given of God “from the beginning of the world, unto man, are the typifying of him.” Typifying means being a type, or symbol, of Him.

deep.intro: Right after the names in Isaiah 9:6, verse 7 tells what kind of King this child will be. Read it, then compare what the angel told Mary in Luke 1:32–33.
deep.q: In Isaiah 9:7, what will have no end?
deep.hunt: In Isaiah 9, what will have no end?
deep.right: The increase of His government and peace
wrong: The wars between Israel and Assyria
The line of kings from Ahaz
deep.why: Verse 7: “Of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end.” Gabriel told Mary the same: “of his kingdom there shall be no end” (Luke 1:33).
deep.find: Of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end

deep.title: From the children’s part of the lesson
deep.intro: The children’s part of this week’s lesson starts with Christmas decorations, like a star, lights or a gift. It suggests verses about a lamb, a star, a shepherd and light, and a song to sing.
deep.q: Which song from the Children’s Songbook does the lesson suggest singing as you look for those symbols?
deep.why: It suggests singing Stars Were Gleaming, from the Children’s Songbook, after talking about how Jesus is like a lamb, a star, a shepherd or a light.

deep.title: From For the Strength of Youth
deep.intro: In a 2022 Christmas article for youth, Elder D. Todd Christofferson lists prophecies of the Savior’s birth, from Adam’s sacrifices to Isaiah, Lehi, Nephi and King Benjamin.
deep.q: According to Elder Christofferson, what have the life and mission of Jesus Christ always been?
wrong: A secret kept from most people
deep.why: He writes that prophets have always taught first of all about Jesus Christ’s life and mission, and that Abinadi said all the prophets since the world began spoke of the Messiah.
deep.find: have always been the central message of prophets

reels.hook: The whole Old Testament was waiting for Him.
reels.body: Isaiah saw a day when God’s people would say, “Lo, this is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us.” That’s this week’s title. From Adam to Malachi, prophets looked forward to the Savior. Isaiah also promised, “He will swallow up death in victory” (Isaiah 25:8). Jesus came, and by rising from the dead He did it. The long wait ended in joy.

verse.text: And it shall be said in that day, Lo, this is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us: this is the LORD; we have waited for him, we will be glad and rejoice in his salvation.

question.q: How do the people in Isaiah 25:9 feel when their God comes?
question.right: Glad: they rejoice in His salvation
wrong: Afraid: they hide from His face
question.why: “We will be glad and rejoice in his salvation.” After the long wait, they meet their God with joy.

bonus.q: In Isaiah 25:8, what will the Lord God wipe away from off all faces?
bonus.hunt: In Isaiah 25, what will the Lord God wipe away from off all faces?
bonus.why: Verse 8: “the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces.” John saw the same promise for the faithful (Revelation 21:4).
bonus.find: wipe away tears from off all faces

reels.hook: The first family on earth already rejoiced in Him.
reels.body: An angel taught Adam that his sacrifices were “a similitude of the sacrifice of the Only Begotten of the Father” (Moses 5:7). Then Adam said, “in this life I shall have joy” (Moses 5:10). Eve was glad too, for “the joy of our redemption.” Long before Bethlehem, the first family knew a Redeemer would come, and it filled them with joy.

verse.text: And Eve, his wife, heard all these things and was glad, saying: Were it not for our transgression we never should have had seed, and never should have known good and evil, and the joy of our redemption, and the eternal life which God giveth unto all the obedient.

question.right: She learned they could be redeemed
wrong: She would never have to work again
She could go back to the garden
question.why: She rejoiced in “the joy of our redemption, and the eternal life which God giveth unto all the obedient.”

bonus.q: In Moses 5:6, an angel asks Adam why he offers sacrifices. What does Adam answer?
bonus.hunt: In Moses 5, an angel asks Adam why he offers sacrifices. What does Adam answer?
bonus.right: He didn’t know; God told him to
wrong: To thank God for the harvest
bonus.why: Verse 6: “I know not, save the Lord commanded me.” Adam obeyed first. Then the angel explained that the sacrifice pointed to the Savior (verse 7).
bonus.find: I know not, save the Lord commanded me

reels.hook: At Christmas we sing about Him. He sings about you.
reels.body: Zephaniah warned of hard days ahead, but he ended his book with a promise: “The LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save.” Then he said the Lord “will joy over thee with singing.” At Christmas we sing carols about the Savior. Zephaniah says He rejoices over His people too, so much that He sings.

verse.text: The LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing.

question.q: How does Zephaniah say the Lord feels about His people?
question.right: He rejoices over them with singing
wrong: He is tired of their mistakes
He watches them from far away
question.why: “He will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love.” He is glad to save them.

bonus.q: In Zephaniah 3:19, who does the Lord promise to save, along with gathering the one driven out?
bonus.hunt: In Zephaniah 3, who does the Lord promise to save, along with gathering the one driven out?
bonus.why: Verse 19: “I will save her that halteth.” Halteth means limps. He saves the ones who struggle, and gathers “her that was driven out.”
bonus.find: I will save her that halteth

reels.hook: The joy the prophets waited for finally came.
reels.body: Isaiah promised that the redeemed would have “everlasting joy” (Isaiah 51:11). The night Jesus was born, an angel brought that joy to shepherds near Bethlehem: “Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people.” Tidings means news. The joy wasn’t just for Israel. It was for all people, and that includes you.

verse.text: And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord.

question.q: Who was the angel’s good news for?
question.why: The good tidings of great joy “shall be to all people.” That includes you.

bonus.q: In Luke 2:19, what did Mary do with all these things?
bonus.hunt: In Luke 2, what did Mary do with all the things the shepherds told?
bonus.right: Kept them and pondered them in her heart
wrong: Told them to everyone in Bethlehem
Wrote them down for the temple priests
bonus.why: Verse 19: “But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart.” To ponder is to think deeply about something.

reels.hook: A prophet hired to curse Israel saw their King coming.
reels.body: Balak, king of Moab, hired Balaam to curse Israel. Instead, the Lord had him bless them. Balaam saw far ahead: “I shall see him, but not now.” A Star would come out of Jacob. Centuries later, wise men came to Jerusalem saying, “we have seen his star in the east” (Matthew 2:2). Jesus calls Himself “the bright and morning star” (Revelation 22:16).

verse.text: I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but not nigh: there shall come a Star out of Jacob…

question.q: Balaam said, “I shall see him, but not now.” What did he mean?
question.right: He saw Someone who would come much later
wrong: He would meet the king of Moab soon
He could see only in the daytime
question.why: He saw a Star “out of Jacob” far in the future, not near: Jesus Christ, born centuries later.

bonus.q: In Numbers 24:17, what else will rise out of Israel besides a Star?
bonus.hunt: In Numbers 24, what else will rise out of Israel besides a Star?
bonus.why: Verse 17: “a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel.” A sceptre is the rod a king holds. The Star would be a King.
bonus.find: a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel

image.alt: Thousands of stars and the Milky Way filling the night sky above a lone tree
image.credit: The Milky Way from Inferno Cone, Craters of the Moon. Photo: NPS / Jacob W. Frank, public domain

reels.hook: His father’s answer pointed to Jesus.
reels.body: Isaac carried the wood up the mountain and asked, “where is the lamb for a burnt offering?” (Genesis 22:7). Abraham answered, “God will provide himself a lamb.” The Book of Mormon says this was “a similitude of God and his Only Begotten Son” (Jacob 4:5). Centuries later, John the Baptist saw Jesus and said, “Behold the Lamb of God” (John 1:29).

verse.text: And Abraham said, My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering: so they went both of them together.

question.q: How was Abraham offering Isaac like Heavenly Father and Jesus?
question.right: A father was willing to give his only son
wrong: A king was sending out his army
A family was moving to a new land
question.why: Jacob called it “a similitude of God and his Only Begotten Son” (Jacob 4:5). Heavenly Father gave His Son for us.

bonus.q: In Genesis 22:13, what did Abraham see caught in a thicket?
bonus.hunt: In Genesis 22, what did Abraham see caught in a thicket?
bonus.right: A ram, caught by its horns
wrong: A lamb, caught by its wool
A goat, caught by its leg
bonus.why: Verse 13: “behold behind him a ram caught in a thicket by his horns.” Abraham offered the ram “in the stead of his son.”
bonus.find: a ram caught in a thicket by his horns

image.alt: Painting of a white lamb lying calmly on a gray table, its feet tied together, against a dark background
image.credit: Agnus Dei (Lamb of God), by Francisco de Zurbarán, public domain

reels.hook: A shepherd boy from Bethlehem knew his Shepherd.
reels.body: David was a shepherd boy, a son of Jesse of Bethlehem (1 Samuel 16:11–18). He wrote, “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.” Want means lack: with Him, we have what we truly need. Centuries later, shepherds near Bethlehem were the first to hear that Jesus was born (Luke 2:8–11). He would call Himself “the good shepherd” (John 10:11).

verse.text: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters.

question.q: What does “I shall not want” mean?
question.right: With Him, I’ll have what I truly need
wrong: I don’t want anything for Christmas
I don’t need a shepherd anymore
question.why: Want here means lack. Like a good shepherd, the Lord leads His sheep to green pastures and still waters.

bonus.q: The Friend’s Christmas program says candy canes can remind us of shepherds. Why?
bonus.right: They look like the sticks shepherds use
wrong: Shepherds ate them on the hills
They are white like a lamb’s wool
bonus.why: It says candy canes look like the sticks shepherds use to lead their sheep. They remind us of the shepherds at Bethlehem and of Jesus, the Good Shepherd.
bonus.find: Candy canes look like the sticks that shepherds use to lead their sheep

image.alt: Painting of Jesus Christ as a shepherd, carrying a lamb in His arms while His flock of sheep walks beside Him
image.credit: The Good Shepherd, by Bernhard Plockhorst. Public domain

reels.hook: Why we fill December nights with lights.
reels.body: Isaiah wrote to people living in dark, frightening times: “The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light.” Matthew says this came true when Jesus lived and taught in Galilee (Matthew 4:13–16). Jesus said, “I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness” (John 8:12). Christmas lights can remind us of Him.

verse.text: The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined.

question.q: Who is the “great light” Isaiah saw coming?
question.right: Jesus Christ, the Light of the World
wrong: A fire on the hills to warn of war
The sun rising after a long night
question.why: Matthew saw Isaiah’s words fulfilled in Jesus (Matthew 4:16), who said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12).

bonus.q: In Micah 7:8, what does Micah say will happen after he falls?
bonus.hunt: In Micah 7, what does Micah say will happen after he falls?
wrong: He will stay down a while
bonus.why: Verse 8: “when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me.”
bonus.find: when I fall, I shall arise

image.alt: The sun rising over snowy mountains, lighting a wide white field of snow with orange and pink
image.credit: Sunrise on the Harding Icefield, Kenai Fjords National Park. Photo: NPS, public domain

reels.body: Isaiah saw a child who would be born and called “Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.” No one name could say all He is. He was already “The mighty God” before He came to earth as a baby. Handel’s Messiah, music many people sing at Christmas, uses these very words. Which of His names means the most to you right now?

verse.text: For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.

question.q: Why did Isaiah give the child so many names?
question.right: No single name could show all He is
wrong: Each of His parents chose some names
People in Judah all had five names
question.why: He is “Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.” Each name shows a different part of who He is.

bonus.q: Isaiah’s own name had a meaning. What does it mean, say the Scripture Helps for Isaiah 1–12?
bonus.why: They say Isaiah’s name means Jehovah is salvation, showing the power of Jesus Christ to save His people. His sons’ names carried messages too.

image.alt: Painting of the prophet Isaiah, an old man with a long white beard

reels.hook: A sign for a king who refused to ask for one.
reels.body: King Ahaz was afraid of two enemy armies. Isaiah told him to ask the Lord for a sign, but Ahaz said, “I will not ask” (Isaiah 7:12). The Lord gave one anyway. Matthew tells us it came true when Jesus was born to Mary, and that Immanuel means “God with us” (Matthew 1:23). At Christmas, God came to be with His people.

verse.text: Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.

question.q: What does the name Immanuel mean?
question.why: Matthew explains: “Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us” (Matthew 1:23). Jesus is God, and He came to live among us.

bonus.q: In Matthew 1:21, why would the baby be named Jesus?
bonus.hunt: In Matthew 1, why would the baby be named Jesus?
bonus.right: He would save His people from their sins
wrong: He would rule over Judah from Jerusalem
He would build a new temple in Zion
bonus.why: Verse 21: “thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.”
bonus.find: he shall save his people from their sins

reels.hook: A little town picked out centuries ahead.
reels.body: Micah named the very town the Ruler of Israel would come from: Bethlehem, “little among the thousands of Judah.” He also said this Ruler’s “goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.” Jesus lived with God long before His birth. When wise men asked where the King was born, the priests and scribes quoted Micah: Bethlehem (Matthew 2:4–6).

verse.text: But thou, Beth-lehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.

question.q: What do the words “from everlasting” tell us about this Ruler?
question.right: He lived long before He was born
wrong: He would rule only a short time
question.why: His “goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.” Before Bethlehem, He was Jehovah, the God of the Old Testament.

bonus.q: The Scripture Helps for Micah say how far Bethlehem is from Jerusalem. About how far?
bonus.why: They say Bethlehem is a small town about five miles, or eight kilometers, south of Jerusalem. Young David lived there too.
bonus.find: about five miles (eight kilometers) south of Jerusalem

insights.title: The chorus of a song
insights.text: “We have waited for him” comes twice in Isaiah 25:9. Donald W. Parry, writing for Scripture Central, notes that this refrain and another repeated line in the next verses suggest the passage is a song. The righteous will sing these words. So this week’s title is the chorus of a song God’s people will one day sing about the Savior who came to save them.
insights.find: The righteous will sing these words

insights.title: So many words for joy
insights.text: Isaiah 9 overflows with joy. Donald W. Parry, writing for Scripture Central, counts four different words for joy in verse 3 alone. Why so much joy? He points to the reasons in the verses after it: the heavy burden is broken, war comes to an end, and most of all, “unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given.”
insights.find: Isaiah employs four words to emphasize the great joy that comes because of Jesus Christ

insights.title: Adam and Eve’s song of thanks
insights.text: Read Adam’s words in verse 10 and Eve’s in verse 11 side by side. Jeffrey M. Bradshaw, writing for Scripture Central, notes that Adam’s words are shaped to match Eve’s. Together, their new understanding and joy make one psalm of thanks. The first family on earth praised God for redemption long before the Redeemer was born.
insights.find: meld to form a harmonious dual psalm of gratitude

insights.title: Joseph’s 1830 manuscript names Jesus Christ
insights.text: Moses 5 came to Joseph Smith as he worked on his revision of the Bible. On this page of his earliest manuscript, in Oliver Cowdery’s handwriting, the Holy Ghost tells Adam, “I am Jesus Christ from the beginning henceforth & forever.” The printed verse says “the Only Begotten of the Father.” Either way, Adam was taught of the Savior by name and title, thousands of years before Bethlehem.
insights.find: the Holy Ghost fell upon Adam which bore record of the Father & the Son saying I am Jesus Christ from the beginning
insights.note: In Joseph Smith’s 1830 manuscript, the Holy Ghost tells Adam, “I am Jesus Christ from the beginning”; the printed verse, our scripture, reads “the Only Begotten of the Father.”

insights.title: Sins washed away like rain
insights.text: “I have blotted out, as a thick cloud, thy transgressions.” Donald W. Parry, writing for Scripture Central, explains the picture: as rain from a cloud cleanses the earth, the Lord wipes our sins clean through His Atonement. The verse also says “return unto me.” In Hebrew, return is one way of saying repent. Repenting means coming back to Him.
insights.find: As the rain from a cloud cleanses the earth

insights.title: The humble, the holy and the wise
insights.text: Who heard first that Jesus was born? President Dallin H. Oaks pointed to three groups. Humble shepherds heard it from angels. Simeon and Anna, holy people at the temple, knew the baby was the Messiah. And wise men came from another land. Because they were from another culture, he said, their witness reminds us the Messiah was born for all people.
insights.find: Those who received the heavenly announcement of the birth were the very humble, the very holy, and the very wise.

insights.title: Don’t leave Him in the manger
insights.text: On followHIM, John Bytheway shares an idea from a Church News editorial by William B. Smart: Christmas has three levels. Level one is the fun of trees, stockings and Santa. Level two is the baby in the manger, the shepherds and the wise men. Level three is the Lord, who suffered for us and rose again. Keep Christ in the manger, Smart warned, and you will be unfulfilled.
insights.find: if you keep Christ in the manger, you’ll be unfulfilled

paras: For their last followHIM Favorites of the Old Testament year, Hank Smith asked John Bytheway for his lesson on the three levels of Christmas. It comes from a Church News editorial by William B. Smart. Level one is the Santa Claus level: reindeer, stockings by the tree, Christmas trees and all the fun. Hank calls it an important part of Christmas, and John agrees: he loves it and watches the Christmas shows like everyone else.

Level two is the Silent Night level: the baby Jesus, the shepherds hearing the angel, the wise men coming. Hank observes that kneeling before the Lord of the universe can feel intimidating, and Christmas lets us come to Him as a little baby. John points to the nativity scenes that remind us of an event “that had been prophesied forever and finally came.”

But Smart added, “if you keep Christ in the manger, you’ll be unfulfilled.” Level three is the Lord level: the resurrected Christ, who suffered for our sins, problems and infirmities, so that we will all live again. Without it, John says, we would not have levels one or two. Hank adds that many people have been born, but no one else has died and come back to life the way He did.

John’s suggestion for this season: as you sing Christmas carols, listen for both levels, words about the newborn Child and words that call Him the Lord and the Savior. Their wish for every listener fits this last week of the Old Testament: a joyous level-one Christmas, a reverent level-two Christmas and a powerful level-three Christmas.
find: Christmas has about three levels and level one is the Santa Claus level
he called it the Silent Night level about the baby Jesus
And that’s the Lord level, he called it.
We hope you have a reverent level two Christmas and we hope you have a powerful level three Christmas.

insights.title: Many symbols, one Savior
insights.text: “The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.” Paul calls Jesus the chief cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). The Old Testament Student Manual explains that the Savior’s life and mission have so many sides that it takes many symbols to show Him: the Lamb, the Light, the Rock, the Good Shepherd, the Cornerstone, the Bright and Morning Star, and more.

source.title: Enrichment Section C: Symbolism and Typology in the Old Testament

insights.find: He is typified or symbolized as the Lamb

insights.title: The Lord will provide
insights.text: After Isaac was spared, Abraham named the place Jehovah-jireh. Jeffrey M. Bradshaw, writing for Scripture Central, explains that a footnote in our Bible gives its meaning as “the Lord will see or provide.” It echoes what Abraham told Isaac in verse 8: God would provide. The Lord provided for Abraham that day, and later God provided His Only Begotten Son.
insights.find: Christians also know that God later provided His Only Begotten Son as a substitute sacrifice

insights.title: A lamb without blemish
insights.text: “Your lamb shall be without blemish.” The Old Testament Student Manual quotes Elder Bruce R. McConkie, who taught that the details of the first Passover were arranged to testify of Israel’s Deliverer. The lamb had to be perfect, with no flaw, because the Lamb of God would be pure and perfect. The lamb’s blood on the doorposts saved Israel, as the Savior’s blood saves the faithful.

source.title: Exodus 11–19: The Passover and the Exodus

insights.find: signifying that the Lamb of God, pure and perfect, without spot or blemish

insights.title: The house of bread
insights.text: Why Bethlehem? President Russell M. Nelson noted that Jesus could have been born anywhere on earth, yet He chose the land He had made holy. He explained that Bethlehem, bet lehem in Hebrew, means “house of bread.” How fitting, he said, that the One who called Himself the bread of life (John 6:35) would come from the house of bread.
insights.find: That word in Hebrew, bet lehem, means “house of bread.”

insights.title: A light for Galilee
insights.text: Isaiah named the lands of Zebulun and Naphtali in northern Israel, where invading Assyrian armies brought dark days. The Old Testament Student Manual explains that this region was later called the Galilee, where Jesus grew up and did most of His teaching. Matthew saw Isaiah’s words come true there (Matthew 4:12–16). The people who walked in darkness saw the “great light” up close.
insights.find: where Jesus was raised and spent most of His ministry

insights.title: A branch from Jesse’s roots
insights.text: On followHIM, Dr. Jeffrey R. Chadwick calls Isaiah 11 the “chief among equals” of the Old Testament’s predictions of Christ. Verse 1 says one thing twice: a rod from the stem of Jesse, a branch from his roots. Jesse was King David’s father, so the branch is a son of David: Jesus. That is why Matthew opens with Jesus’ family line through David.
insights.find: It is the chief among equals

paras: Dr. Jeffrey R. Chadwick, a BYU professor of archaeology and Near Eastern studies, told Hank Smith and John Bytheway that of all the Old Testament passages this week’s lesson suggests, Isaiah 11 jumped out at him. In his view it is “the chief among equals” of the Old Testament’s predictions of Christ, though not everyone sees it that way.

He explains that Isaiah 2 through 12 is one great unit. It opens with the great prophecy of the temple in Isaiah 2, moves through events in Israel’s history that point toward the coming Messiah in Isaiah 11, and closes with a song of victory in Isaiah 12, “the Lord Jehovah is my strength.” Nephi focused on this same block of Isaiah in 2 Nephi 12–24.

Verse 1 is a synonymous parallel, Isaiah saying the same thing twice with different words. A rod, the limb of a tree, comes from the stem, the lower trunk, of Jesse; a branch grows out of his roots. Jesse was the father of David, so both lines point to a Messiah from David’s family. “This is Christ. This is Messiah. This is Jesus,” he says.

That, he adds, is the message of the genealogy at the start of Matthew: Jesus, born in Bethlehem, came from the line of David going back to Abraham. It is why people who loved Jesus called out to Him as the Son of David. He also notes that Latter-day Saints read Isaiah 11 with help from Doctrine and Covenants 113.
find: Isaiah chapter two through Isaiah chapter 12 is one entire unit
You have here what we call a synonymous parallel where Isaiah is saying the same thing with synonyms saying it twice.
Jesse was the father of David, right?
that whole genealogy of Jesus is to demonstrate that Jesus, born in Bethlehem, was of the lineage of David going back to Abraham

insights.title: God with us, in the flesh
insights.text: Donald W. Parry, writing for Scripture Central, notes that Immanuel is a Hebrew word meaning “God with us.” He says the name teaches two things at once: Jesus is God, and He came down to live among us in the flesh. In Doctrine and Covenants 128:22, He is even called the King Immanuel.
insights.find: Immanuel emphasizes that Jesus is God

insights.title: Why He is called the everlasting Father
insights.text: Jesus is the Son of God, so why does Isaiah call Him “The everlasting Father”? The Old Testament Student Manual shares an explanation from the First Presidency and the Twelve in 1916. Under the direction of His Father, Jesus Christ created the heavens and the earth. As the Creator, He is rightly called the Father of heaven and earth.
insights.find: Jesus Christ, being the Creator, is constantly called the Father of heaven and earth

insights.title: Peace in Christ, even now
insights.text: Elder Quentin L. Cook calls “Prince of Peace” one of the Savior’s most cherished titles. He points out that peace in the whole world isn’t promised until the Second Coming. But each of us can have personal peace now, even when the world is angry and divided, by following Christ and doing the “works of righteousness.”
insights.find: personal peace can be achieved despite the anger, contention, and division

insights.title: Salvation, and the name of Jesus
insights.text: “Behold, God is my salvation.” Donald W. Parry, writing for Scripture Central, points out that salvation is the main theme of this short song: the word comes twice in verse 2 and again in verse 3. He adds that the Hebrew word for salvation, yshu‘ah, is also the name of Jesus in Hebrew.
insights.find: is also the name of Jesus in Hebrew

insights.title: His name, written out
insights.text: In the King James Bible, the Lord’s name Jehovah usually appears as LORD in capital letters. The Old Testament Student Manual points out that Isaiah 12:2 is one of the few places the name is written out in full, and lists this verse as another: “whose name alone is JEHOVAH.” Jehovah, the God of Israel, is Jesus Christ.
insights.find: This is one of the few times the name is written out fully as Jehovah in the King James translation.

insights.title: Born in a tiny village
insights.text: President Henry B. Eyring points out that Jesus could have been born into any situation the Father chose. In fulfillment of Micah’s prophecy, He was born in a tiny village in the hill country of Judea. Humble shepherds welcomed Him, wise men followed a star, and rulers feared Him. He chose to come down from His throne out of love for each of us.
insights.find: Jesus could have been born into any situation the Father chose

insights.title: Titles found only in Moses
insights.text: “I am Messiah, the King of Zion, the Rock of Heaven.” Jeffrey M. Bradshaw, writing for Scripture Central, points out that some of the Savior’s titles in Enoch’s vision, like the King of Zion and the Rock of Heaven, appear only in the book of Moses. Messiah, he notes, means the Anointed One.
insights.find: appear only in the book of Moses

insights.quote: For us, there is nothing new in the celebration of the birth of Christ. The message is timeless and familiar. It was taught to Adam. It was preached to the children of Israel.
insights.text: The angel’s “good tidings” were not new news. President Oaks reminds us that prophets taught the same message from Adam on.

insights.quote: Old Testament prophets from Adam to Malachi are testifying of the divinity of the Lord Jesus Christ and our Heavenly Father.
insights.text: Verse 9: the Holy Ghost taught Adam of the Only Begotten. President Kimball says every prophet after him testified of the Savior too.

insights.quote: The message of the Old Testament is the message of Christ and his coming and his atonement
insights.text: The lesson points to these verses: He bore our griefs and was wounded for our sins. President Romney sums up the whole Old Testament in one line.

insights.quote: We may not be captive in Egypt or Babylon, as were the ancient Israelites, but we are captive nonetheless—captive to sin and death.
insights.text: Verse 1 promises “liberty to the captives.” President Eyring explains who the captives are today, and why the birth of Jesus is good news for them.

insights.quote: Christmas is joyful not because it is a season or decade or lifetime without pain and privation, but precisely because life does hold those moments for us.
insights.text: Verse 8 promises that the Lord will swallow up death and end sorrow. President Holland explains why Christmas joy is real even in hard times.

source.title: That Babe in the Manger Makes All the Difference

insights.quote: At the birth of Him who is called the “bright and morning star,” a new star appeared in the heavens.
insights.text: Balaam saw “a Star out of Jacob.” President Nelson ties the new star at Jesus’ birth to one of the Savior’s own titles (Revelation 22:16).

insights.quote: He was both the Lamb and the Shepherd. At the birth of Him who is called the “good shepherd,” shepherds were the first to receive the announcement of His holy birth.
insights.text: Psalm 23 calls the Lord a shepherd. President Nelson notices who heard first that the Good Shepherd was born.

insights.quote: Jesus Christ was the Great Jehovah, God of the Old Testament. He was the promised Immanuel.
insights.text: Isaiah promised a son called Immanuel. President Nelson testifies who that child was, long before He was born.

insights.quote: It is wholesome and proper to look for similitudes of Christ everywhere and to use them repeatedly in keeping him and his laws uppermost in our minds
insights.text: Moses 6:63 says “all things bear record of me.” Elder McConkie invites us to look for symbols of Christ everywhere, like the ones in this week’s lesson.

source.title: Enrichment Section C: Symbolism and Typology in the Old Testament

insights.title: The Birth of Jesus (Bible video for children)
insights.text: A three-minute Bible video for children from the Church, telling the story of Jesus’ birth. Watch for the town where He is born, and remember that the prophet Micah named it centuries before (Micah 5:2).

video.title: The Birth of Jesus: A Bible Story for Children
